text: Six weeks on the new medication and today, for the first time, I noticed the morning. Not endured it, noticed it. The light on the kitchen wall, the sound of Rafi's bike going past, the fact that the coffee tasted of coffee. For two years mornings have been something to get through with my eyes half shut, and I'd stopped expecting that to change, I'd made peace with it being the weather of my life. The doctor said give it eight weeks and I nodded the way you nod at things you don't believe. I'm not fixed. There'll be flat days, she was clear about that. But I stood at the sink this morning and thought, oh, there you are, and I'm not sure whether I meant the day or me. Either way. I've put the next appointment in the calendar with a small sun next to it.

The shop's been open a month and today we broke even. Not profit, break even, the magic line where the till covers the rent and the stock and Giulia's wages and leaves nothing over for us. But it's the line everyone said we wouldn't reach until the spring, and we reached it in February, in the rain, on a Tuesday. I did the numbers three times. Giulia did them a fourth. Then we locked the door and sat on the floor behind the counter with the emergency bottle and didn't even open it, just sat there grinning at the shelves. Nine months of savings gone. Our flat full of boxes. My parents still convinced we've lost our minds. Maybe. But the line is real and we're on the right side of it and for the first time since we signed the lease I can see a version of next year where this works. I'm going to sleep like a stone.

Kwesi spoke to me first today. Four months of me talking to the back of his head, four months of grunts and closed doors and plates left outside the room, and this afternoon he came into the kitchen, leaned on the counter the way he used to, and asked if I'd heard about the thing with the football. That's all. The thing with the football. I said no and he told me, properly told me, with his hands going, and I made tea and didn't say anything that could be read as a question, and we stood there for twenty minutes. Then he went back upstairs. The counsellor said it would come in inches and it would come sideways and I should take the inches. I'm taking it. I'm sitting here holding it like a bird. I know tomorrow might be a door again. But he leaned on the counter. He wanted to tell me something. That's not nothing. That might be everything.

Planted the apple tree today, the one we bought the week we moved in and then left in its pot by the back door for a year because there was always something more urgent. It's not much, a stick really, with four leaves and a label. The man at the nursery said five years before you get fruit worth eating. Five years. I stood in the hole with the spade and thought about where we'd be in five years and for once the thought didn't scare me: the mortgage down a bit, Lior in secondary school, maybe the extension, maybe not. It felt like putting a flag in the future and saying, we'll be here. Lior helped tread it in and asked if we could name it. We named it Keith. I don't know why. I keep looking out of the window at a stick called Keith and feeling oddly certain about things.

The surgeon said the word 'successful' and I've been repeating it in my head like a prayer. They got all of it. Margins clear. There's radiotherapy to come and it won't be a picnic and she was careful to say the next two years of scans matter. But all of it. I walked out of that office and the corridor looked different, wider, as if someone had turned up the lights. Bilal was waiting by the vending machine pretending to read a poster about hand hygiene and when I nodded he made a noise I've never heard him make. We sat in the car and didn't drive anywhere for a while. There's a version of this year I'd been quietly preparing for and I get to put it down now. Not all the way down. But I can see the road again and it goes somewhere. I'm going to plant bulbs this weekend. Something that comes up in spring.

The flat viewing went well. Actually well, not 'well considering'. Third floor, two rooms and a kitchen with a window that looks over the allotments, and the landlord is a retired teacher who asked more about my cat than my salary. If I get it, and she said she'd let me know by Thursday and she smiled when she said it, I'll be out of Marcus's spare room by the end of the month. Six months on a sofa bed. Six months of being grateful and in the way at the same time. I walked back along the canal afterwards and I was, I realised, planning. Where the bookshelf would go. Which route to work. A plant for the windowsill. I haven't let myself plan anything since the split because planning felt like asking to be disappointed. I'm asking. Thursday. I've written the landlord's name on a sticky note so I don't jinx it by saying it out loud.

Eleven months sober and today I wasn't white-knuckling it. I walked past the Crown at six with the doors open and the smell of it and the noise, and I noticed it, and I kept walking, and my hands were in my pockets instead of balled up. Last summer that walk would have taken everything I had. I'm not cured. I know how this works, I've read the stories, I know month eleven is where people get cocky and fall. I'm not cocky. I'm just noticing that something that was a wall is now a hill. Kasia asked me tonight what I want for my one-year and I said I didn't know, and then I said actually I'd like to go back to the coast, the place we went when the kids were small, and she said okay, like it was a normal thing to want. It is a normal thing to want. I'm starting to think I might get to want normal things.

Tao came to the table tonight. Voluntarily. Sat down, ate, didn't bring the phone, and when Mina told her story about the hamster he actually laughed. Three months since the diagnosis and I've been reading everything, joining the groups, learning the words, and the thing nobody tells you is how much of it is just waiting for your kid to come back into the room. Tonight he came into the room. The new school's doing something right, or the meds are, or he's just fourteen and fourteen shifts like weather. I'm not going to ask which. I'm going to let it be a Wednesday where my son ate dinner with us and laughed at a hamster. Afterwards he said 'night' from the stairs without being prompted. I'm writing it down because I want to be able to find it again on the days he doesn't.

Week six of the renovation and I've stopped being able to tell which day it is. We're living in the one room that still has a door, the three of us and the dog, eating off the ironing board. The builders start at half seven, which means I'm up at six to move the car and the dog and the child, and they finish at four, which means I spend the evening hoovering plaster dust off every surface so the child doesn't eat it. I had a shower at the gym today because ours is a hole. Amira says it'll be worth it, and she's right, and I don't have the energy to agree out loud. My back is a fist. I fell asleep at my desk at three this afternoon with my hand on the mouse and woke up to an email from Saad asking if I was okay. I'm okay. I'm just made of sawdust. Eleven more weeks. Don't tell me that.

Six nights of night shifts and then straight into Mum's hospital appointment this morning because there was nobody else. I drove there on autopilot, I genuinely don't remember the roundabouts, and sat in the waiting room with my eyes closed pretending to think. The consultant asked me a question and I said 'sorry?' three times. Mum was lovely about it. She kept patting my knee and telling the nurses I work too hard, which was mortifying and true. Got her home, made her lunch, got back here at two and lay down on top of the covers in my coat for what I meant to be ten minutes. It's dark now. The coat's still on. I've got a headache sitting behind my eyes like a stone and the thought of making dinner makes me want to lie back down. I'll have toast. I'll sleep until the alarm and then do it all again. I'm not sad. I'm just worn down to the wire.

The twins have both got the cough. Not the dangerous one, the doctor says, just the kind that goes on for a fortnight and peaks at two in the morning. So for five nights now Leni and I have been doing shifts, one up with whichever twin is barking, the other getting maybe three hours in a row if lucky. I put my keys in the fridge this morning. I turned up at nursery on Tuesday with no nursery, it was Monday. I wrote an email at work that was, I discovered later, entirely in lower case and signed with the wrong name. My body feels like it's been borrowed by someone heavier. Leni fell asleep standing up against the kitchen counter tonight while waiting for the kettle and I didn't wake her, I just stood next to her and leaned too. The cough will pass. Everyone says so. I'd just like to remember what it was like to think in full sentences.

Marking. Ninety-four scripts, each one between six and nine pages, each one deserving of real attention and each one receiving, by this point, whatever attention I have left. Started at eight this morning, finished at half ten tonight with a break for a sandwich I ate over the pile. My eyes feel like someone's rubbed them with a towel. I've written 'good point, develop this' so many times it's lost all meaning as a phrase. Oyelaran's handwriting alone took eleven minutes. There's a stack of forty more for tomorrow and a department meeting at nine that will be about the marking load, which is funny in a way I can't currently appreciate. I love teaching. I want that on the record, somewhere, on a day I'm not this spent. Tonight I just want to lie down in a dark room where there are no words at all, and particularly no essays about the French Revolution.

Got in from the airport at one in the morning after the Singapore trip and the taxi driver had to wake me at the door. Four days, three time zones, eleven meetings, two of which I'd happily have done over email. My body thinks it's lunchtime. The flat was cold because I'd turned the heating off, which was sensible, and I stood in my coat waiting for the radiators and couldn't remember whether I'd eaten on the plane. I've unpacked exactly one thing, the charger. The suitcase is in the hall where I dropped it and it can stay there until the weekend. Hanne left a note on the counter saying the meeting moved to nine tomorrow and I read it twice and it still says nine. I'm going to sleep in my clothes. I'm thirty-nine and I'm going to sleep in my clothes with the light on. Nothing is wrong. I just have nothing left.

Dad's funeral was today and I've got nothing left. Not grief, I did that last week when it happened and I'll do more of it later, I know that. Today was the admin of grief. Shaking hands with people I half knew, saying thank you for coming two hundred times, making sure the sandwiches came out and the slideshow worked and Auntie Nkechi got a lift home. I held it together for Mum. I held it together for the speech. I held it together through the man from his old firm who talked for fifteen minutes about golf. And now I'm sitting on the edge of the bath with my shoes off and I couldn't tell you my own phone number. Everything in me feels used up. Tolu's run me a bath and I'm grateful and I don't think I can lift my arms to get in it. Tomorrow there's the solicitor. Tonight I'm just going to sit here in the steam.

The deadline moved three times this month and each time it moved towards me. Finished the final draft at four this morning, sent it, slept for two hours, got up, did the school run with my eyes mostly closed, did the client call where I'm fairly sure I agreed to something, and have now been staring at the same spreadsheet cell for twenty minutes. The coffee's stopped working. I've had five and I just feel jittery and flat at the same time. Dagny asked at lunch if I was ill and I said no, just tired, and she said I looked like I'd been exhumed, which was fair. Everything is a bit far away. Sounds arrive late. I keep losing the thread of what I was doing between standing up and getting to the other side of the room. I'll be in bed by eight if I can make it to eight. I'm not sure I can make it to eight.

Seventeen hours on the ward because Maria called in sick and the agency couldn't send anyone till the night shift. Two admissions, one discharge that took four hours of paperwork, a man in bed six who kept pulling his line out, and the daughter of the lady in bed two who needed, quite rightly, an hour of someone's time, and the someone was me. I ate a packet of crisps at the nurses' station at three and that was lunch. I got home and sat in the car for a while because walking to the door seemed like a lot. Pavel had kept dinner warm and I ate about half of it with my coat still on. My feet don't feel like feet. There's a hum in my ears. I'm not upset about any of it, that's the job, I chose it, I'd choose it again. I'd just like my body back for a night. I'm on again at seven.

Read the review tonight. Two stars, four paragraphs, and every one of them about a restaurant that isn't mine. He says the lamb was dry. We don't serve lamb. He says the waitress was rude and names a woman who left eight months ago. He says he came on a Saturday and we're closed on Saturdays. I know because I'm the one who's there on the other six days, from eight in the morning till past midnight, for a place that is just about keeping its head above water, and some man with a username and a grudge has knocked us down a whole star on the site every new customer checks first. I've reported it. The site says it may take up to thirty days. Thirty days. Beatriz says don't read them. I'll always read them. I built this place with my own hands and some stranger gets to lie about it in public and I have to be polite about it. I've been pacing for an hour. I could put my fist through the wall.

My brother used Mum's card again. Four hundred pounds, this time, on something he says was 'an emergency', from a woman on a pension who doesn't check her statements because she trusts him. She trusts him. I found it because I set up the alerts last year after the last time, and I sat at my desk at work watching the notification and I had to go outside. He'll cry when I ring him. He always cries. He'll promise. And she'll forgive him, because she's his mother and because she's frightened of what happens if she doesn't, and I'll be the hard one again, the one who makes a fuss about money. I'm not making a fuss about money. I'm making a fuss about a grown man stealing from his mother and everybody agreeing to call it something else. I rang Dov and he said calm down before you call him, and I'm trying. I've been trying for an hour. I'm not calm.

The referee's decision wasn't the thing. The thing was the parent on the touchline who screamed at my daughter, a nine-year-old, for 'diving', and then when I went over and asked him calmly to stop, told me to teach her to play properly. I've never wanted to hit someone before. I mean that literally; I'm forty-four and I've never felt it in my hands like that. I didn't. I walked back to the car and sat there until my pulse came down while Ana finished the game and scored, actually scored, with her bottom lip out. The club's got a code of conduct that nobody enforces. I'm writing to them tonight. I'm writing to the league. I've got his car registration, which I'm aware is a bit much, and I don't care. You do not scream at children. You do not scream at my child. My hands are still not quite steady on the keyboard.

The agency sent me a 'performance improvement plan' today. Me. The person who covered three people's work through the whole of the spring while they were 'restructuring', who did the Dawson pitch alone over a weekend and won it, who hasn't taken a sick day in two years. The plan says my 'collaborative energy' has been low. It was written by Hollis, who has been in the role for eleven weeks and has had precisely one conversation with me, during which he asked how to work the coffee machine. I read it in the toilets so nobody would see my face. I don't shout at work. I didn't shout. I went back to my desk and did my job for the rest of the day with my jaw clamped so hard it aches now. Collaborative energy. I've started writing down everything I did this year, with dates. If they want a paper trail they can have mine.

They cut the tree down. The oak at the end of the lane, the one that's been there longer than any of the houses, the one with the rope swing the kids on the estate have used for thirty years. The developer said it was diseased. It wasn't diseased. Nadia's husband is a tree surgeon and he looked at the stump tonight and said there was nothing wrong with it except that it was in the way of six executive homes. They did it at seven in the morning on a Tuesday before anyone could object, which tells you everything. I stood at the stump with about a dozen neighbours and nobody said much. Old Mr Doyle had tears in his eyes. I'm not a protest sort of person. I've never written to a councillor in my life. I've written to three tonight. I've found the planning reference. They can build their houses but they're going to hear about this first.

Caught Jonas going through my phone. Not glanced at, not picked up by mistake: sitting on the edge of our bed, scrolling my messages, with the look of someone who'd been doing it for a while. He says he was worried. He says I've been distant. I have been distant, because I've been dealing with my dad's diagnosis, which I told him about, which he apparently didn't think was the whole story. Twelve years. Twelve years and he thinks the answer to 'she seems sad' is to read her texts to her sister. I didn't shout. I took the phone and I went for a walk and I'm still out, sitting on the bench by the war memorial in the cold, because if I go home now I'll say something that can't be put back. I'm so angry I feel calm, which I know isn't the same thing. He's texted four times. I haven't read them. He can see how that feels.

Found out today that the reason my proposal got turned down in March was that Jeremy had told the committee, in a side conversation I wasn't part of, that I 'wasn't ready to lead something of that scale'. He has never worked with me. He has never seen me lead anything. He has, I'm told, played squash with the chair. I've spent eight months thinking the idea wasn't good enough. I rewrote it twice. I lost sleep. I apologised to my team for not getting them the funding. And all along it was a man who's never read a page of my work deciding what I'm ready for over a drink. I'm not going to do anything rash. I've learned that much. But I've requested the minutes, and I've booked time with the chair, and I'm going to ask her, very politely, exactly what was said. The politeness is going to cost me everything I've got.

The council has approved the application for the takeaway under our flat despite forty-one objections, a petition, and the fact that the planning officer's own report said the extraction would vent directly beneath our bedroom window. Forty-one objections. They 'noted the concerns'. We'll have the smell of fried chicken in our pillows by October and a queue of people shouting outside at midnight, and the compensation for that, apparently, is nothing, because we're tenants and tenants are weather. Oluwaseun went to the meeting and said the committee barely looked up. He said one of them was on his phone. I pay my council tax. I vote. I filled in their consultation form in full sentences with footnotes. And I might as well have posted it into the sea. I'm going to find out who's on that committee. I'm going to be at every meeting they hold from now until they're sick of my face.

Wednesday. Nothing special about it and I want to write it down because of that. Walked Sadie to school and she told me about a book with a dragon in it for the whole way and I didn't check the time once. Worked from the kitchen. Dmitri rang at lunch to say nothing in particular and we talked about the garden for ten minutes. In the afternoon I finished the thing I've been putting off and it wasn't as bad as I'd made it. Pasta for dinner, the one with the lemon. Sadie did her reading on my lap even though she's too big for it now and we both know it. The house is tidy enough. The bills are paid. Nobody's ill. I used to think I'd only be allowed to feel like this once I'd achieved something, and it turns out it's just available, on a Wednesday, if you stop looking past it. I'm going to go to bed early with the dragon book.

We finished the fence. Three weekends, one trip to A&E for a splinter that turned out to be nothing, and a lot of swearing at the post-hole digger, but it's done and it's straight, mostly, and Priya and I stood at the kitchen window tonight with a cup of tea looking at it like it was the Taj Mahal. The garden feels like ours now. The dog can't get into next door's veg. The neighbours waved over the top of it, which is exactly the right height for waving. There's nothing dramatic about a fence. I'm aware of that. But I've spent my whole adult life renting places I wasn't allowed to put a nail in, and tonight I put forty posts in the ground on land with my name on it, with the person I love, and the tea tasted like tea, and that'll do. That'll absolutely do.

Sunday evening and for once the dread hasn't turned up. The week ahead is just a week. Work's fine, properly fine, not the 'fine' I used to say through my teeth at the old place. I've got the review on Wednesday and I'm not frightened of it. Marguerite's got her choir thing on Thursday and I'm going to go and sit at the back and be bored and happy. The fridge is full. The washing's done. I made a lasagne big enough for three dinners and I'm quietly pleased with it. I'm sitting on the step with the last of the light and the cat is doing something complicated with a moth. Six months ago I couldn't have imagined being this unremarkable and this okay. I don't need the week to be good. I just need it to be ordinary, and I think it will be, and that's the whole of what I want tonight.

Grandad's ninetieth today, in the garden, with all of us. Four generations round two trestle tables that didn't match, a cake that leaned, children under the table feeding the dog sausage rolls. He didn't make a speech, he never does, he just sat in the good chair with a glass of something and watched us all like we were a film he'd been waiting to see. At one point I caught his eye across the table and he raised his glass about an inch and I raised mine back and that was the whole conversation. Everyone I love was in one place. Nobody argued. Nobody's ill. The weather held. I know that won't always be true, I know it's a kind of luck as much as anything, but tonight, washing up with Chidi while the little ones slept on the sofa in a heap, I just felt full. Full and fine and here. Ninety. The old boy's done all right.

Last day of the holiday and I'm not sad about going home, which is new. Two weeks in a cottage with no signal, long walks, bad weather, a lot of cards. Ewan read four books. I read two and a half and slept more than I have in a year. We didn't do anything you could put in a postcard. The most exciting thing was a seal. And tonight, packing, I realised I'm not clinging to it the way I usually cling to the end of a holiday, like it's the last good thing before the grey. I'm going back to a life I actually like. The flat, the job, the Tuesday swim, the people. The holiday was lovely and the life is lovely and I've not been able to say both of those at once before. The seal was good though. I'll give the seal that.

Paid off the last of the loan today. Set up the transfer, pressed the button, got the little tick. Seven years. I thought I'd feel like celebrating and instead I just felt settled, like a chair that's finally got all four legs on the ground. No more juggling. No more doing the sums in my head in the supermarket queue. I'm not rich. I'm nowhere near. But the money that comes in is now money that's mine, all of it, for the first time since I was twenty-three, and the quiet of that is lovely. I didn't tell anyone. I made a nice dinner, the fish, and had a glass of wine on the balcony, and watched the lights come on across the estate. Felipe rang and asked what I was up to and I said nothing much. It was true. Nothing much. It was perfect.

Another evening of the old routine and I notice I've stopped wanting it to be more. Walk the dog by the river. Pick up bread. Make the soup from whatever's in the drawer. Read in the chair with my feet on the stool while the radio mutters. Call Mum at eight, same as every day, talk about her neighbour's shed and the price of things. Bed by ten. I used to think this was what you did while you waited for your real life to start. It's taken me till fifty-three to notice that the waiting was the thing that was in the way, not the routine. The soup was good tonight. The dog found a stick she was very pleased with. Mum laughed at something I said. That's a day. That's a good day. I don't know why it took so long to see it, but I see it now, and I'm not giving it back.

Mal's final checkup was clear and we celebrated by doing absolutely nothing. He'd wanted a party. I'd wanted a party. And then we got home from the hospital and sat down on the sofa and neither of us got up for about four hours. Takeaway from the Lebanese place. A film we'd both seen. His head on my shoulder going heavy around nine. A year of appointments and fear and being brave at each other, and it ends not with fireworks but with two tired people on a sofa under a blanket that needs a wash. Good. That's good. I don't need the fireworks. I spent the year wishing for boring and tonight I got boring and I'm holding it with both hands. He's snoring now. The dog's snoring too. I'm going to sit here a bit longer and let it be this simple.

Everyone else in the office has somebody to text when something funny happens. I noticed it today. Someone did a ridiculous thing with the printer and six people reached for their phones at once, and I did too, out of habit, and then I didn't have anyone to send it to. I'd have sent it to Petra. Petra's in Auckland now and it was four in the morning there. I'd have sent it to Mum, once. I ate lunch on the bench by the car park, which I've started doing because the kitchen is loud with other people's plans. I'm not unhappy at work. I like the job. It's just that eight hours a day I'm surrounded by people and I'm somehow the only one who goes home to a flat where the loudest thing is the fridge. I put the radio on when I get in now. I've started talking to the fridge. It's a nice fridge. It doesn't talk back.

The village is beautiful and I knew nobody when we moved and I still know nobody, six months on, and tonight that landed. Youssef's at the hospital four nights a week, which is the whole reason we came, and I'm here with the view and the quiet and the wood burner and the complete absence of anyone who'd notice if I didn't leave the house. I've tried. I went to the quiz, I went to the thing at the church hall. People are friendly in the way that means hello at the shop. Back home I'd have walked round to Amal's and sat in her kitchen and complained about nothing. Here I walked to the end of the lane and back in the dark and the only person I passed was a man with a dog who nodded. I rang Amal. She was out. Of course she was, she has a life, I used to be in it. The fire's gone out. I can't be bothered to relight it.

First Christmas since Dad went and the kids are at their mum's this year, it's her turn, it's fair. I'd planned to be fine. Volunteered at the shelter in the morning, which was good, I'll do it again. Then home at two to a flat that was exactly as I'd left it, and a turkey crown for one that I couldn't be bothered to cook, and the Queen's speech on with nobody to talk over it. I rang the kids and they were sweet and busy and had a lot of new things. I rang my sister and got the voicemail. I sat in the chair Dad sat in last year, in his paper hat, telling the same joke, and I'd give a great deal to hear that joke again. It's eight o'clock. I've had three mince pies and a glass of the good stuff and the telly's talking to itself. I'm not going to ring anybody else. Everybody's somewhere. I'm here.

The group chat has been going all evening about the weekend, the one I wasn't invited to. Not pointedly, I don't think. I just wasn't thought of. There was a time I'd have been the one organising it. Then I had Seb and couldn't come to things for a while and then I could and nobody asked and now it's been long enough that asking myself would be strange. I watched the little dots and the photos and the in-jokes I don't understand any more and I put the phone face down and I picked it up and I put it down. Seb's asleep. The house is quiet in that specific way. I love him so much it hurts and I would not trade a minute of him and I am also, tonight, so starved of grown-up company that I had a ten-minute conversation with the Amazon driver about the weather and was sorry when he left.

Uni was supposed to be the bit where you find your people. Term two and I'm still eating in my room. The flat's fine. They're nice. They go out together on Wednesdays and they ask me and I say maybe and then I don't, because the one time I went I stood at the edge of a kitchen for two hours holding a can and nobody noticed when I left. Lectures are big and nobody talks. The society I joined meets at a pub I can't afford. I FaceTimed Mum tonight and did the voice, the everything's-great voice, and she bought it, or pretended to. Then I lay on the bed and looked at the ceiling and listened to them all laughing through the wall. I don't know what I'm doing wrong. Everyone else seems to have been handed a manual. I've started counting the days till Easter, which is not what you're supposed to count.

Bruno's away for the month and I'm discovering how much of my life was just him being in the next room. Not talking, even. Just the sound of him typing or the kettle going or the door at six. I'd thought I'd enjoy the space, I'd planned things, I was going to do the course and see Nadira and sort the loft. I've done the course. I haven't seen Nadira, she's got the baby. The loft is still the loft. Mostly I come home and the house is exactly as I left it, every cushion, and I eat standing up and go to bed early because there's nothing to stay up for. It's two more weeks. I'm embarrassed by how long two weeks looks. I'm a grown woman with a job and friends and a library card and I'm counting sleeps like a kid at boarding school. I've started leaving his jumper on the chair just so the room isn't so tidy.

Ninety-one and the last of my friends went this week. Doreen, from the hospital, we trained together in fifty-four. The funeral's Thursday and Ade will drive me and it'll be full of her grandchildren who don't know me. I've been to so many of these now that I know the order of service by heart. The thing nobody warns you about getting old is not the knees or the forgetting, it's that you become the only one who remembers. There is no one left alive who knew me at twenty. No one I can say 'do you remember' to about anything before about 1990. Ade's good to me, the carers are kind, the girl from the library brings the large print. But they know a nice old lady. They don't know Peggy who danced on the tables at the Palais. I don't know where she went either, most days. I've got the photographs. Photographs don't laugh at the same things.

The match went to three in the morning my time and I watched it alone in the kitchen with the sound down so I wouldn't wake Lotte. We won. We actually won, on penalties, and I jumped up and punched the air and then stood there in the dark with nobody to grab. Back home the whole street would be out by now. Dad and my uncles would be hoarse. The phone's full of messages from people I grew up with and I've replied to all of them and it's not the same as being in a room where everyone smells of the same beer. I love this country. I chose it, I'd choose it again. But there are moments it's very clear I'm living on a different clock from everyone who knew me first, and three in the morning in a quiet kitchen with the best result in twenty years is one of them. I ate a bowl of cereal. I went to bed. Nobody to tell.

The shed is finished. I know. A shed. But I built it myself, from a drawing I did on the back of an envelope, with wood I cut, with a roof that doesn't leak, I checked in the rain last night like a maniac with a torch. Six weekends. Two trips back to the timber yard because I measured wrong. One smashed thumb. Noor said at the start that I should just buy one, which was sensible, and tonight she stood inside it and said 'this is actually good' in a voice of genuine surprise, and I'll be dining out on that tone for a decade. The door shuts properly. The window opens. I put a chair in it and sat there this evening with a beer while the light went and thought: I made this. Me, who couldn't put up a shelf three years ago. I know it's a shed. It's my shed. I keep going out to look at it.

I didn't drink at the wedding. All day, from the champagne at the ceremony to the thing at midnight where everyone does shots, with Cousin Rashid pushing a glass at me every half hour because 'one won't hurt', and it would, and I know that now, and I said no each time without explaining and without apologising. Eight months ago I couldn't get through a Tuesday. Today I danced sober at my sister's wedding and made a speech people laughed at and remembered all of it, every bit, including her face when she saw the cake. I drove home. I drove home! Zainab fell asleep in the passenger seat and I had the road and the radio and the whole clear-headed night and I kept thinking: you did that, you did the hardest day on the calendar and you did it as yourself. I'm not going to make a fuss. I'm just going to write it down so it's real.

Amaya's recital was tonight and she played the piece. The hard one, the one with the run in the middle that she's been swearing at since Easter, the one I'd privately decided she should swap for something easier and then kept my mouth shut about. She walked out, bowed too fast, sat down, and played it clean. Not perfect. There was a wobble near the end and her foot went wrong on the pedal. But clean, and brave, and when she stood up her face was pink and furious and thrilled all at once. I clapped so hard my hands hurt. She's eleven. She practised every single day, including the days she cried about it, including the day she slammed the lid and said she hated it and then came back twenty minutes later. I didn't do that. She did that. I just drove her there and shut up. I'm so proud of her I could burst, and I'm a little proud of the shutting up.

Handed in the dissertation at eleven fifty-two. Eight minutes to spare, which is on brand. Twelve thousand words, two years of evening classes after work, more weekends in the library than I'd like to count, and a chapter on policy frameworks that I'm fairly sure nobody will ever read voluntarily. I'm forty-six. I left school at sixteen. My dad told me university was for other people and I believed him for twenty-five years. Tonight I walked out of that building with the receipt in my hand and sat on the wall outside and I didn't cry, exactly, but my eyes went. Wen had put a bottle in the fridge with a note that said 'DR' with a question mark and I laughed out loud alone in the kitchen. It's not a doctorate, it's a master's, I told her, and she said 'yet'. It's done. I did it. Nobody can un-do it.

The crew finished the house on time and under budget and nobody got hurt. That's the whole entry really, but I want to say it properly because I've been doing this for twenty-two years and it's rarer than you'd think. Seven months. A client who changed her mind about the stairs twice. A winter that flooded the site in January. Two lads on their first job who could've gone either way and went the right way, and one of them, Finlay, laid his first clean course of brick on Tuesday and stood back from it like he'd painted a chapel. I taught him that. Tonight the client walked through with her mum and her mum cried in the kitchen, and the client shook my hand with both of hers. I'm not a sentimental man. I went and sat in the van for a bit. That's a good house. That's a house that'll be there when I'm not.

The kids put on the play. The one I've been running after school since September, with a cast of fourteen eleven-year-olds, half of whom couldn't look at the audience in October. Tonight the hall was full, parents on folding chairs, the headteacher in the front row, and they did it. Lines dropped, a sword broke, the donkey fell off the stage and climbed back on and got the biggest laugh of the night. Ruby, who hasn't spoken above a whisper in class all year, said her speech to the back wall and the back wall heard every word. Afterwards they came off bouncing, all talking at once, and a boy I've had to ask to sit down roughly four hundred times this year hugged me round the middle and said 'Miss, we did it'. We did. I'm not paid for this. I'd do it for free again tomorrow. I'm so proud of those kids I can't see straight.

My daughter stood up to him. Fifteen years old, in the middle of the kitchen, calm as anything, and told her father that the way he speaks to me isn't okay and she's not going to pretend she doesn't hear it any more. I'd never have done that at fifteen. I'd never have done that at thirty-five, which is partly how I ended up here. He went quiet. Then he left the room, which is his version of losing. She turned round and her hands were shaking and she said 'was that okay' and I said yes, baby, that was more than okay. I'm not proud of the house she's grown up in. I'm ashamed of a lot of it. But something in her came out straight despite all of it, and I think, I hope, some of that straight came from me. I've booked the appointment with the solicitor for Thursday. I should have done it years ago. She just showed me how.

The piece went up today. Four thousand words, my name under the headline, in a paper my grandfather used to read at the kitchen table with his glasses on his forehead. It's about the estate where I grew up and I spent five months on it and got it right, I think, got it kind and true at the same time, which was the whole of the difficulty. Mum's bought six copies. Mrs Adeyemi from the fourth floor, who I interviewed, rang this morning in tears to say I'd made her sound like herself. That's the one that got me. Not the editor's email, though that was nice. A woman I grew up underneath saying I'd heard her properly. I've wanted to do this since I was nine. There were a lot of years where it looked like I wouldn't. I'm going to sit here with the paper for a bit before I'm humble about it.

Twenty-three unread in the work inbox, nine in the personal, a text from the school about costumes for Friday, a voicemail from Mum's GP, a reminder that the car tax runs out Thursday, and a message from Esme asking if we're still on for the thing I'd forgotten we'd arranged. I made a list. The list has thirty-one items. I made the list to calm down and it had the opposite effect. I don't know how everyone else does this. I look at the other mothers at the gate and they seem to have the same number of hours I do and they have time to do their hair. I've been standing in the kitchen with a cold cup of tea for twenty minutes trying to decide between the car tax and the costume and I can't, I actually can't, my brain has just filled up like a sink. Vik gets back at nine. I'm going to hand him the list and go and sit in the car.

Started the new course on Monday and by today I'm drowning. Four modules, each with its own portal, each with its own login, each with a reading list longer than anything I did at school. The lecturers talk as if we all did the pre-reading and I didn't know there was pre-reading. I missed a deadline today I didn't know existed because it was in a 'module handbook' I didn't know existed. Everyone in the seminar seemed to know each other already. I sat in the car park afterwards with the laptop open on my knees trying to work out what was due when and I couldn't make the dates line up, there were just too many tabs, and I closed the lid and sat there. Dilan rang and I let it ring. I'm twenty-nine and I feel like I've been dropped into the deep end of something I thought I'd be good at. I don't know which thing to do first. There's no first.

Both parents in two different hospitals forty miles apart. Dad's hip on Tuesday, Mum's fall on Thursday, and I'm the only one of us within three hundred miles, so I've done four round trips in three days and I've got a bag in the car with both their reading glasses in it and I've started labelling things. The ward won't tell me anything on the phone so I have to be there. Work's been understanding, by which they mean they've emailed to ask when I'll be back. The dog's at Hamza's. The kids are with their dad an extra night. Tonight I stood in the hospital car park trying to remember which hospital I was at and I had to look at the sign. I'm not crying because there's no time slot for it. I've got Dad's discharge meeting at nine and Mum's scan at eleven and they're forty miles apart and I'll make it work because there's nobody else, and then I'll do it again on Saturday.

The launch is in nine days and three of the five people who were building it have left. Not fired, left, for better money, within a fortnight of each other, and the work they were doing is in their heads and in a handful of folders nobody else can make sense of. I'm now the project manager, the lead developer, the person who answers the client, and the person who explains to the board why the thing they announced in the newsletter might not exist by the date in the newsletter. I've been in the office until eleven four nights running. My inbox has stopped being a list and become a wall. Today Sana asked a simple question about the data model and I opened my mouth and nothing came out, just nothing, I stood there like a laptop with the beachball spinning. I'm not panicking. I don't have time to panic. I just have twelve things that are all the most urgent thing.

Three children, one bathroom, a dishwasher that died on Sunday and a babysitter who cancelled this morning for the nativity I'm meant to be at and the meeting I'm meant to be at, which are at the same time, in different towns. The nursery has sent four forms. The school has sent three. The youngest has nits again. The oldest needs a Victorian costume by Friday and I don't know what a Victorian child wore because I didn't have time to be one. Jon's away until Thursday with work and he's doing his best and his best is a text that says 'sounds hectic babe'. I sat on the stairs tonight with the lice comb in one hand and the school email open in the other and I just couldn't choose. Nits or Victorians. Victorians or nits. I'm still sitting here. The house is doing that thing where every room has a job in it and I can't walk into any of them.

Moved countries on Monday and today is Thursday and I've already lost the ability to think. New language, new currency, a bank account I can't open without an address and an address I can't get without a bank account. The furniture's in a container somewhere between here and there. The school wants documents I've never heard of. The phone doesn't work properly. I spent two hours in a government office today being sent between three desks by three people who were each very kind and each said a different thing. Bao's doing the job he came for and loving it and I'm glad for him and I also want to scream a bit. I came home to the empty flat with the mattress on the floor and I sat on it and stared at the plug socket, which is the wrong shape, obviously, everything's the wrong shape, and I didn't move for an hour. Tomorrow the internet man comes, between eight and six.

Christmas is in eleven days and I've agreed to host both families, which seemed loving in October and seems unhinged now. Fourteen people. Three vegetarians, one coeliac, my brother who's just gone vegan 'to see', Nana who won't eat anything green, two toddlers and a dog that bites. The oven's small. The table isn't a table so much as two tables and a door. I've got a spreadsheet for the food and a spreadsheet for the sleeping and a note on my phone that just says 'CHAIRS???'. Work doesn't stop because I've lost my mind, so I've been doing the planning at midnight, and tonight I opened the food spreadsheet and all the cells swam and I shut the laptop and put my head on it. Ellis says cancel, order in, nobody would mind. Everybody would mind. I'd mind. I just can't currently see the shape of how it happens. I'll see it tomorrow. Please let me see it tomorrow.

Took over the shop from Dad on the first and it's the twentieth and I'm underwater. He ran it from his head. Thirty years of suppliers and favours and 'ring Tony on a Wednesday, not a Thursday', and none of it written anywhere. The till system is from 2009. The accountant speaks a language I don't. Three regulars have asked where he is and when I say retired they look at me like I've killed him. I've been here from six to eight every day and the stock room is still a mystery and I've just found a drawer of unpaid invoices going back to the spring. Mei came in tonight with food and found me sitting on a box of crisps staring at a delivery note, and she didn't say anything, she just sat on the next box. I can't see the whole thing. I can only see the next invoice and the next and the next. Dad rang to ask how it's going and I said great.

Logging the week so I've got it for the appraisal. Monday: client call with Aditi, agreed the scope, sent the summary by four. Tuesday: half day, dentist at two, nothing needed. Wednesday: all-day workshop, nothing came of it except the follow-up on the data question, which I've put on Karl. Thursday: wrote the first draft of the Q3 report, about two-thirds through, sent the structure to Aditi for a sanity check. Friday: team meeting at ten, agreed holiday cover for August, took an hour on the expenses backlog, which is now clear. Still open from last week: the vendor contract, waiting on legal; the dashboard access, waiting on IT; the one-to-one with the new starter, booked for Monday at eleven. Hours this week around forty-two. Next week: finish the report, start the budget template, remind Karl about the data question on Wednesday if nothing's come back.

Garden notes, mid-April. Broad beans came up on the sixth, about eighty percent, so the mice got the rest. Sowed the second row of peas and the first carrots, the short ones, in the raised bed. Potatoes went in last Saturday: twelve seed potatoes, the red ones, in the bottom bed with a bucket of compost each. Moved the rhubarb crown that's been in the shade, it may sulk for a year. Pruned the apple, lightly, probably later than ideal. Compost bin number two is ready to turn out. Still to do: net the strawberries before the blackbirds notice, buy more canes, fix the water butt tap which drips. Weather's been dry for ten days, watered the beds on Tuesday and Friday. Soil temperature in the top bed was twelve degrees this morning. Fatima's offered some tomato seedlings next week, she's got too many again. Will take six.

Hospital notes for Mum so I can tell Raj. Admitted Sunday night via A&E, chest pain, kept in for observation. Monday: blood tests clear, ECG showed something they want to look at more closely, consultant is Dr Mensah, she said it's 'not urgent but not nothing'. Tuesday: echo scan done at two, results to the consultant by Thursday. They've started her on a low dose of something for blood pressure, the name's on the sheet in the folder. She's on ward 14, bed by the window, visiting is two till eight. Needs: her own pillow, the big-print crossword book, her reading glasses which are in the kitchen drawer, the charger for the old phone not the new one. Discharge likely Friday if the results are fine, with a follow-up in clinic in about six weeks. Parking is cheaper in the multi-storey than the hospital car park. The café shuts at four.

Writing down the recipe before I forget how I did it, because Lukas asked. Onions, two, cooked slowly in butter for about twenty minutes until soft, not brown. Then garlic, three cloves, and a spoon of the paste, cooked out for a minute. A tin of tomatoes, a tin of chickpeas with the water, a tin of coconut milk. Spinach at the end, a big bag, it looks like too much and isn't. Salt, more than you think. Lemon juice at the end. It simmers for about twenty-five minutes once everything's in. Served it with rice and the flatbreads from the Turkish shop. It made enough for four with a portion left over, which is in the freezer in the blue box. Could use a bit more heat next time, maybe a chilli with the garlic. Lukas thought it wanted more lemon. Total time about an hour. Cost about six pounds for everything.

House move checklist, six weeks out. Done: solicitor instructed, survey booked for the fourteenth, mortgage offer received and valid until the end of next month. Movers: three quotes, going with the middle one, deposit paid, provisional date the twentieth subject to exchange. Utilities: electricity and gas final readings to be taken on the day, new supplier for the new place set up to start the same day. Broadband: cancellation given, new install booked for the day after the move, twelve till four. Post redirect: set up for six months. Still to do: change the address with the bank, the DVLA, the GP, the dentist, the kids' school, the car insurance, and whatever else turns up in the post over the next month. Boxes: twenty so far, probably need forty. Mirela's offered the van for the plants and the awkward things. Keys: collect from the agent after one on the day.

Training log, week nine. Monday rest. Tuesday: six miles easy, fifty-four minutes, left calf tight for the first mile then fine. Wednesday: intervals, eight by four hundred, around ninety seconds each, with two-minute jogs between. Thursday rest, foam rolled the calf. Friday: five miles steady, forty-two minutes, felt good. Saturday: long run, fourteen miles, two hours ten, took a gel at mile seven and another at eleven, fine, no stomach issues. Sunday: short recovery jog, three miles, with Jerome, chatting pace. Total for the week about thirty-four miles. Shoes are on roughly three hundred and ten miles, will need replacing before the race. Weight stable. Sleep average about seven hours. Next week is the last big one before the taper: long run goes to sixteen. Need to book the sports massage for the week after and order the gels, the lemon ones, not the orange.

Minutes of the residents' meeting, as best I can remember them, because nobody else took any. Present: eleven of us, plus the man from the management company, Gavin. Agenda item one, the bins: the collection has moved to Wednesdays, the bin store door lock is being replaced next week, and the fly-tipping behind block C has been reported to the council with a reference number Gavin will circulate. Item two, the lift: the engineer has been out twice, the part is on order, the estimate is three weeks. Item three, the service charge: up four percent, breakdown to be emailed. Item four, the garden: Hilde has offered to organise a working party for the beds, date to be agreed, probably a Sunday in May. Any other business: the front door closer is slow and someone keeps propping it with a brick. Next meeting in three months. Biscuits were provided by number nine.

Notes from the car service so I've got them for next time. Dropped it off at eight, collected at half four. Full service done, oil and filter, air filter, pollen filter. Front brake pads were at about thirty percent, replaced, discs are fine for now. Rear tyres have about four millimetres, front ones about three, so the fronts will want doing before winter. Advisory: slight play in the nearside front wheel bearing, not urgent, keep an eye on it, probably a job for the next service. The noise I'd mentioned on cold starts is the auxiliary belt, they've tensioned it, if it comes back it needs replacing. Battery tested fine. Wipers replaced. Total came to just under the quote. Next service due in twelve months or ten thousand miles, whichever first. MOT is due in March. Sven at the garage said to ring in February to book both together.
